title: The FBI Raided the Wrong House. The Number Was on the Mailbox.
title_candidates: The FBI Raided the Wrong House. The Number Was on the Mailbox.
Six Agents Broke Down the Wrong Door. Nine Years Later, Still No Trial.
description:
At five in the morning on 18 October 2017, a six-member FBI SWAT team broke down the front door of a house on a corner lot in south-west Atlanta. A woman was asleep inside. Her seven-year-old son was asleep across the hall. The warrant they were carrying was for a different house, three or four doors away.

The address of the house they had just entered was on the mailbox at the end of the driveway, outside, where anybody could have read it. The Supreme Court of the United States later described what happened in one sentence: only after the team was inside did another officer stumble across some mail with the home's address on it, and realise they had the wrong house.

This film follows what happened after the door. The family sued under the Federal Tort Claims Act — the statute Congress amended in 1974, after a pair of wrong-house raids in Collinsville, Illinois, precisely so that innocent people raided by federal officers would have someone to sue. A district court dismissed the case. A federal appeals court affirmed. In June 2025 the Supreme Court ruled for the family, unanimously, and sent the case back — and the family still has not had a trial. In March 2026 the Eleventh Circuit heard the case again, on remand, and as of this film it has not ruled.

Nobody has been found liable. No damages have been awarded. No jury has heard a word of it.

Every quotation on screen is from the record: the opinion of the Court, Justice Sotomayor's concurrence, and the transcript of the oral argument of 29 April 2025.

This is general history, not legal advice. Some imagery is AI-assisted and symbolic — a reconstruction, not authentic footage, and no real person's likeness is depicted.
